vignette:
He was twenty-six when he first stepped off the cargo plane. The heat hit him like a wall, and the dust smelled of diesel and something burnt. He had signed up with a small relief organization, partly out of a vague sense of moral duty, partly because his life back home-apprenticing with a jeweler in a quiet downtown shop-had begun to feel too small, too safe. He wanted to prove something to himself. For the first three months, he helped distribute food packs and medical supplies. He learned to work fast and stay low. He learned the sound of a mortar before it lands. He learned not to look too long at the children.

The day that changed everything started with a routine convoy. They were delivering water to a village that had been cut off. He remembers the dust on the windshield, the radio crackling in Arabic, the driver's hand tapping nervously on the steering wheel. Then the world compressed into a single roar. He doesn't remember the explosion itself, only the after: the taste of copper in his mouth, the ringing in his ears, the way the light seemed wrong. He helped pull the driver from the wreckage. The driver's leg was gone below the knee, and he was screaming in a language that didn't need translation. For a long time after, no one came. He sat in the rubble with three children who had been playing by the road. One of them was still alive when the medics arrived.

Now he is twenty-nine. He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment above a jewelry shop in a mid-sized city. He works at a bench under a bright lamp, repairing broken clasps and resetting stones. His hands are steady when they need to be-the fine motor control came back after months of practicing on old watch movements-but his body betrays him in other ways. Two or three times a week, a door slams in the shop downstairs, and he finds himself on the floor, heart hammering, before he knows what happened. He has stopped going to the grocery store during peak hours. Crowds feel like pressure, like the seconds before an event he can't predict. He scans every face for signs of anger or desperation.

He does not watch the news. He avoids any documentary about conflict zones, even fictional war movies. When an old colleague calls to check in, he lets it go to voicemail. The messages pile up until he deletes them without listening. He tells himself he is not ready, and then he forgets to ever feel ready.

At night, he dreams of dust and a ringing silence. Sometimes he wakes with the name of the driver on his lips-Elias-a man he never saw again after the evacuation. He has not cried since that day. He feels, most of the time, like he is wrapped in heavy gauze. The world reaches him muffled. He knows he should feel grateful to be alive, that he came home, that his hands still work. But gratitude is a word without weight. When a customer lingers too long at his bench, watching him work, his chest tightens. He wants to be invisible. He wants the quiet to stay quiet.

He has not dated since returning. The idea of explaining what he saw, or not explaining it, feels exhausting. At a party six months ago, a friend's casual joke about a loud car backfiring sent him diving behind a sofa. He left without saying goodbye. He has stopped going to parties.

On good days, the work absorbs him. He can lose himself in the geometry of a setting, the precise pressure of a jeweler's saw, the cool weight of metal in his palm. On bad days, a stray sound-a siren, a helicopter overhead-drops him back into the dust, and he spends the rest of the shift staring at his own hands, trying to remember the way home.
